newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi urges talks with China over sovereignty row.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi urges talks with China over sovereignty row.

text.p: Vietnam on Thursday reiterated its claim to sovereignty over an offshore area where China is exploring for gas and called for negotiations to resolve the dispute.

"As we have clearly stated, the area where the Kan Tan III rig is operating completely lies within Vietnam's exclusive economic zone and on the continental shelf," a Foreign Ministry spokesman told a news conference.
"At the same time, we always advocate resolving disputes through diplomatic channels. Vietnam advocates solving all disputes through negotiations," the spokesman said.
"Parties concerned should exercise self-restraint, doing nothing to further complicate the situation or resort to the use of force or threats."

He said Vietnam wished that for the sake of friendship between the two countries and peace and cooperation in the region, its legitimate demand would result in a positive response and draw support from regional and world opinion.

Vietnam said last weekend it had protested to China, demanding immediate withdrawal of the Kan Tan III drilling rig and accompanying vessels from an area 64.5 nautical miles off its central coastline.
It said coastguards had repeatedly sent warnings after the oil rig and vessels arrived on March 7 in an area Vietnam calls Block 113. However, drilling operations continued.
In its response to the protest, Beijing said the rig was in Chinese waters and that its activities were beyond reproach.
The two nations have competing claims on areas along their land border, on parts of the Tonkin Gulf and on the Paracel Island chain, which lie east of the latest area of dispute.
They are also among six regional claimants to the Spratly Islands, which are further to the south.
Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) ambassadors in Hanoi said on Thursday they had been called by the Foreign Ministry to an urgent briefing on the issue.
Vietnam joined ASEAN in July 1995, which analysts said could strengthen its hand in any sovereignty disputes with China.
However, one ambassador said ASEAN countries were likely to see the latest row as a bilateral issue to which the association would not add its voice.
"We don't want to have a general ASEAN reaction," he said. "It's better left to the two countries."
ASEAN comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
